html:
The penal law code of the Tang dynasty, first issued in 624 and revised in 627 and 637. The version issued in 652 had 502 articles in twelve sections, and an official commentary followed in 653. It is the oldest Chinese law code that survives complete.

The code blended two older traditions. From the Legalists, such as Han Fei, it took fixed written laws and set punishments. From Confucius and his followers it took the idea that law should uphold the family and social rank. Crimes against parents or superiors were punished harder than the same crimes against equals or juniors. Punishments came in five grades, from beating with a light stick to death.

It was backed by civil statutes and rules for officials, and it built on codes of the Sui and earlier northern dynasties.

Its reach went far beyond the Tang:

  • Later Chinese codes, through the Song to the Great Ming Code and the Qing code, followed its structure.
  • Japan's Taiho Code of 701 was modelled on it.
  • Korea and Vietnam drew on it for their own laws.

For more than a thousand years, it set the shape of law across East Asia.
